Section V — Treatment in Preadolescent Children (skeletal): What's Different?
  • Skeletal correction is now essentially restricted to the mixed dentition, with a 2nd phase in adolescence (early correction relapses with continued growth in the original pattern). Transverse expansion is more physiologic before adolescence; Class III maxillary protraction is easiest before age 11 (or with skeletal anchorage in adolescence).
  • Compressive force on the condyle hasn't shown lasting growth restraint, but force at the sutures above/behind the maxilla in adolescence can redirect/restrain maxillary growth. Vertical growth stops last (late teens girls, early 20s boys) → both long- and short-face patients need prolonged retention.
Growth Modification in the Transverse Plane
  • Compare maxillary width to the patient's own proportions (e.g. bizygomatic), not population means — a narrow maxilla + narrow mandible + normal occlusion is not a problem. Beware diagnosing a transverse deficiency when it's really an AP deficiency. Opening the suture hinges the maxilla (apex at the nasal bridge) and opens more anteriorly.

I Primary / Early Mixed Dentition

  • Three methods: (1) split removable plate (slow, low force; less cost-effective); (2) lingual arch (W-arch / quad-helix) — a few hundred grams, slow, ⅓ skeletal / ⅔ dental; (3) fixed jackscrew expander (bulky; rapid activation can distort the face in young children). Preferred: slow expansion with an active lingual arch.

II Late Mixed Dentition

  • A fixed jackscrew (banded/bonded) Fig 13.4; include as many teeth as possible (wait for first premolars if primary molar roots are resorbed). Vertical-height increases are transitory. A bonded (occlusal-coverage) appliance suits a long-face tendency (less mandibular rotation). Either rapid or slow is acceptable; slow (<2 mm/week over 10–12 weeks) gives a similar result with less trauma Fig 13.5.

III Adolescents (Early Permanent Dentition)

  • Near-100% chance of opening the suture in mid-adolescence; as the spurt ends, interdigitation may make it impossible. Suture-maturation guides: chronologic/dental age, CVMS, the 5-stage method (none validated).
New · assessing & expanding the mature suture
  • Midpalatal suture density ratio (MSDR) from CBCT (Grünheid et al.) was the only method significantly correlated at a clinically useful level for judging whether the suture can still be opened.
  • For mature patients, don't attempt tooth-supported expansion — use micro-implant–assisted palatal expansion (MARPE), one screw activation (0.25 mm) per day; otherwise SARPE (surgically-assisted) or segmental osteotomy. Skeletal anchorage works better in adolescents (bone maturity).

IV Rapid Palatal Expansion — details

  • 0.5 mm/day (two quarter-turns) → ≥1 cm in 2–3 weeks, with 10–20 lb across the suture. The suture space fills with fluid/hemorrhage (highly unstable) → stabilise & leave in place 3–4 months for bone to fill; the midline diastema closes (skeletal relapse + stretched gingival fibres, not tooth movement alone). After retention, a removable palatal retainer guards against relapse Fig 13.8 (or a transpalatal/heavy auxiliary wire).

V Slow Palatal Expansion & alternatives

  • <2 mm/week → ~2 lb (mixed dentition), opening the suture near the max bone-formation rate (no diastema). After 10–12 weeks ≈ the same skeletal/dental result as RPE (RPE gives more across the canines).
  • Alt-RAMEC (Liou — alternate weekly expand/constrict with a double-hinged expander, then facemask) aims to disrupt the lateral/posterior sutures too — but cannot be recommended for protraction (changes not clinically different from routine expansion).
  • Implant-supported expansion — palatal bone screws give better anchorage and significantly less tooth movement; the goal is to load the bone, not the teeth (ideal in anodontia/severe hypodontia, or to maximise skeletal change). With skeletal anchors use slow expansion; hinged designs expand more anteriorly Fig 13.10. Retention rule: keep the fixed device 3–4 months, then a tooth-supported retainer 6–12 months.

VI Expansion & Sleep-Disordered Breathing

New RPE increases nasal/nasopharyngeal volume (sometimes ~2× on CBCT) and usually lowers nasal resistance. In sleep-disordered breathing without adenotonsillar hypertrophy, RPE reduces the AHI and arousal index — even with tonsillar hypertrophy, a decreased AHI was sustained at 36 months.Linked · Ch 6/7 OSA But routinely expanding a normal palate into buccal crossbite just for breathing is questionable — justified only with demonstrated nasal-airflow resistance.

VII Clinical Management

  • Four-band devices give more transverse expansion/arch perimeter than two-band — band the first premolars if available. Expansion creates dental interferences → the mandible rotates down & back, and face height almost always increases permanently (posterior eruption). Use a bonded expander in long-face/open-bite patients (the splint resists posterior eruption — weak evidence); for deep bite, expander type makes no difference.

VIII Transverse Mandibular Constriction  ·  IX Restriction of Transverse Growth

  • The mandible has no midline suture (fused early) → true expansion needs distraction osteogenesis (greater anteriorly; condyles rotate slightly, no lateral movement — well tolerated). Restricting excessive transverse growth is almost impossible; a lingual arch holds molar width only. For a wide mandible + normal maxilla, the best option is usually to tolerate a posterior crossbite that causes no mandibular shift (no functional/esthetic reason to correct it).
Class III Growth Modification

I Concepts

  • Class III ≈ any combination of deficient maxillary + excessive mandibular growth (about equally likely). Chin-cup force against the cranium causes more down-back mandibular rotation than true restraint. Class III elastics between bone anchors are now the most effective growth-modifying method orthodontics has ever had.

II Maxillary Deficiency (AP & vertical)

Three approaches, in order of effectiveness:

FR-III functional appliance

  • Mandible positioned posteriorly/open, pads stretch the upper lip Fig 13.13; mostly dental change (maxillary molars erupt down/mesial, occlusal-plane rotation → Class I) Fig 13.15. Little/no effect on maxillary deficiency — mild cases only, with long treatment/retention.

Reverse-pull headgear (facemask) — dental anchorage

  • True skeletal change declines after age 8; clinical success after 10–11 Fig 13.16. Tooth movement is inevitable. Hooks in the canine–primary-molar area above the occlusal plane put the force near the maxilla's center of resistance and limit rotation Fig 13.17–13.18. Best for minor-moderate problems; defer until first molars/incisors erupt. Palatal expansion is compatible (a useful splint) but not needed just to improve protraction. ~350–450 g/side, 12–14 h/day; slight downward traction if vertically deficient (contraindicated if face height is large). 25–33% recur by 8 years later from excessive mandibular growth (not maxillary relapse).

Facemask to skeletal anchorage · Class III elastics to miniplates

New · bone-anchored maxillary protraction
  • Facemask to miniplates on the anterior maxilla gives more skeletal change than dental anchorage (≈ 4–5 mm advancement is the limit), but miniplate placement is invasive and bone maturity isn't adequate until ~age 11.
  • Class III elastics to maxillary & mandibular miniplates (De Clerck, 2010) — the most effective protraction; light force to the jaws, not teeth. Three-screw plate at the zygomatic buttress + two-screw plate on the anterolateral mandible Fig 13.21 (mandibular plate after the canines erupt, ~age 9; adequate bone density ~age 11). Best plan: ~1 year between ages 12–14; ≤250 g/side (often 150 g), steady force. Don't remove the plates for 6–12 months after debond (late Class III growth). Facial change exceeds anything previously seen in ~⅓ of patients, with opening of the zygomaticomaxillary/zygomaticofrontal sutures Fig 13.24. Forward maxillary movement does not help the airway (sleep apnea is not an indication).
  • vs facemask: Class III elastics gave ~2.5–3 mm more maxillary movement; midface changes occurred in 32% of the elastics group vs none with facemask.

III Mandibular Excess

  • Functional appliances make no pretense of restraining growth — they rotate the mandible down/back and camouflage (lingual lower incisors, facial upper); rotate 3–5/6 mm beyond rest (more = too severe for functionals).
  • Chin cup Fig 13.26 — only transient restraint (overwhelmed by later growth); rotates the chin down/back (↑ face height), often uprights lower incisors (soft cups more so). Once accepted as rotation (not inhibition), lighter force for greater rotation makes sense. Ineffective because growth modification needs light long-duration force, but chin cups deliver heavy short-duration force.
  • Class III elastics to skeletal anchors (De Clerck) — four mandibular effects: chin back 4–5 mm (in some), condylar-fossa modeling, increased mandibular length with the chin staying put (growth expressed as backward condylar movement) Fig 13.28, and mandibular bending limiting chin advance Fig 13.29. The largest effect is still forward maxillary growth (not ideal for true prognathism).
  • Summary — controlling excessive mandibular growth is orthodontics' greatest challenge: functionals and chin cups offer only down-back rotation (risking a long face); Class III elastics from miniplates now genuinely change the mandibular growth pattern (lack of forward growth in ~80%, possible chin retrusion, ↑ gonial angle) and, treating both jaws, are an improvement over modifying one.
